messages.author: 17d1c8192f4bc4be
messages.subject: code taking too long to run under stan2.01
parts:
Dear all,

I have the following latent variable model I am trying to fit in stan. I think I can use vectorization somewhere in my code, but I am not sure. I would like to know, for example, if I can use vectorization in poisson_log? Feel free to comment in the code what part can be made faster and where I can get ride of loops. Thank you!  

Bcca_mod <- '
data   {
int<lower=1> N; // sample size
int<lower=1> n1;
int<lower=1> n2;
int<lower=1> d;
int X[n1,N];
int Y[n2,N];
}
parameters {
real<lower=0> bet[d];
real<lower=0> sig_te;
real<lower=0> sig_lb;
matrix[d,N] Z;
matrix[n1,d] A; 
matrix[n2,d] B; 
matrix[n1,N] teta;
matrix[n2,N] lambd;
real mux[n1];
real muy[n2];
}
transformed parameters {
matrix[n1,N] mu_te;
matrix[n2,N] mu_lb;
real<lower=0> sigte_sr;
real<lower=0> siglb_sr;
real<lower=0> beta_sqt[d];
mu_te <- A*Z;
mu_lb <- B*Z;
siglb_sr <- sqrt(sig_lb);
sigte_sr <- sqrt(sig_te);

for(i in 1:d)
beta_sqt[i] <- sqrt(bet[i]);
}
model {

for(i in 1:n1)
mux[i] ~ normal(0, 1000);

for(i in 1:n2)
muy[i] ~ normal(0, 1000);

bet ~ inv_gamma(2, 1);
sig_lb ~ scaled_inv_chi_square(10, .1);
sig_te ~ scaled_inv_chi_square(10, .1);

for(i in 1:d)
Z[i] ~normal(0, 1);

for(i in 1:n1)
A[i] ~ normal(0, beta_sqt);

for(i in 1:n2)
B[i] ~ normal(0, beta_sqt);

for(j in 1:N)
{
for(i in 1:n1)
{
teta[i,j] ~ normal(mu_te[i,j] + mux[i], sigte_sr);
X[i,j] ~ poisson_log(teta[i,j]);  
}
for(k in 1:n2)
{
lambd[k,j] ~ normal(mu_lb[k,j] + muy[k], siglb_sr);
Y[k,j] ~ poisson_log(lambd[k,j]);
}
}
}
'

On 10/29/13 12:05 PM, maxwell wrote:
> Dear all,

> I have the following latent variable model I am trying to fit in stan. I think I can use vectorization somewhere in my
> code, but I am not sure. I would like to know, for example, if I can use vectorization in poisson_log? Feel free to
> comment in the code what part can be made faster and where I can get ride of loops. Thank you!
>
> Bcca_mod <- '
> data {
> int<lower=1> N; // sample size
> int<lower=1> n1;
> int<lower=1> n2;
> int<lower=1> d;
> int X[n1,N];
> int Y[n2,N];
> }
> parameters {
> real<lower=0> bet[d];
> real<lower=0> sig_te;
> real<lower=0> sig_lb;
> matrix[d,N] Z;
> matrix[n1,d] A;
> matrix[n2,d] B;
> matrix[n1,N] teta;
> matrix[n2,N] lambd;
> real mux[n1];
> real muy[n2];
> }
> transformed parameters {
> matrix[n1,N] mu_te;
> matrix[n2,N] mu_lb;
> real<lower=0> sigte_sr;
> real<lower=0> siglb_sr;
> real<lower=0> beta_sqt[d];
> mu_te <- A*Z;
> mu_lb <- B*Z;
> siglb_sr <- sqrt(sig_lb);
> sigte_sr <- sqrt(sig_te);
>
> for(i in 1:d)
> beta_sqt[i] <- sqrt(bet[i]);
> }
> model {
>
> for(i in 1:n1)
> mux[i] ~ normal(0, 1000);

You can vectorize this to

mux ~ normal(0,1000);

But do you really have data at the scale where you expect
mux to be in the thousands? If not, tightening the prior can
help.

> for(i in 1:n2)
> muy[i] ~ normal(0, 1000);
>
> bet ~ inv_gamma(2, 1);
> sig_lb ~ scaled_inv_chi_square(10, .1);
> sig_te ~ scaled_inv_chi_square(10, .1);

I'm not good enough to know what problems might crop up from
these priors.

> for(i in 1:d)
> Z[i] ~normal(0, 1);
all of these are vectorizable.

>
> for(i in 1:n1)
> A[i] ~ normal(0, beta_sqt);
>
> for(i in 1:n2)
> B[i] ~ normal(0, beta_sqt);

Here, you can use

A_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

A <- beta_sqt * A_raw;

The second step can be local or implicit.

> for(j in 1:N)
> {
> for(i in 1:n1)
> {
> teta[i,j] ~ normal(mu_te[i,j] + mux[i], sigte_sr);

You can vectorize this if you transpose mu_te, as

teta[i] ~ normal(mu_te[i] + mux, sigte_sr);

But again, you can apply the non-centered representation (aka,
the "Matt trick"). This is described in the manual.
> X[i,j] ~ poisson_log(teta[i,j]);

Yes, you can do:

X[i] ~ poisson_log(teta[i]);

> }
> for(k in 1:n2)
> {
> lambd[k,j] ~ normal(mu_lb[k,j] + muy[k], siglb_sr);
> Y[k,j] ~ poisson_log(lambd[k,j]);
> }
> }
> }

The issue may be more related to the sampling than to the speed.
Are you getting good numbers of effective samples per iteration?

- Bob

the initialization and the first couple of random steps.

I'd try something a little less ambitious than 80,000
or I'd reduce the refresh so you can see the progress happening.

Did running for 1000 lead to such low sample size that you
thought you'd need 80,000 to get enough effective samples?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] code taking too long to run under stan2.01
parts:
This is usually indicative of your step size being too large (as has been discussed many times on the list if you search the archives).
Try lowering your step size, which is probably easiest by setting the adapt delta to 0.9 or even 0.99.

Why do you need 80000 samples, anyways? Is your autocorrelation that poor?

messages.author: 17d1c8192f4bc4be
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] code taking too long to run under stan2.01
parts:
Bob, 
In your previous email you made recommendations on ways to vectorize some instead of using loops. I go some questions regarding some of your recommendation (see below)

> for(i in 1:n1) 
> A[i] ~ normal(0, beta_sqt); 
> 
> for(i in 1:n2) 
> B[i] ~ normal(0, beta_sqt); 

Here, you can use 

   A_raw ~ normal(0, 1); 

   A <- beta_sqt * A_raw;
A is a n1xd matrix and beta_sqt is a vector of d elements. Or simply put, elements in a given column of A have the same normal distribution. Does your suggestion still hold?
On Tuesday, October 29, 2013 1:10:28 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:

On 10/29/13 12:05 PM, maxwell wrote:
> Dear all,
>
> I have the following latent variable model I am trying to fit in stan. I think I can use vectorization somewhere in my
> code, but I am not sure. I would like to know, for example, if I can use vectorization in poisson_log? Feel free to
> comment in the code what part can be made faster and where I can get ride of loops. Thank you!
>
> Bcca_mod <- '
> data   {
> int<lower=1> N; // sample size
> int<lower=1> n1;
> int<lower=1> n2;
> int<lower=1> d;
> int X[n1,N];
> int Y[n2,N];
> }
> parameters {
> real<lower=0> bet[d];
> real<lower=0> sig_te;
> real<lower=0> sig_lb;
> matrix[d,N] Z;
> matrix[n1,d] A;
> matrix[n2,d] B;
> matrix[n1,N] teta;
> matrix[n2,N] lambd;
> real mux[n1];
> real muy[n2];
> }
> transformed parameters {
> matrix[n1,N] mu_te;
> matrix[n2,N] mu_lb;
> real<lower=0> sigte_sr;
> real<lower=0> siglb_sr;
> real<lower=0> beta_sqt[d];
> mu_te <- A*Z;
> mu_lb <- B*Z;
> siglb_sr <- sqrt(sig_lb);
> sigte_sr <- sqrt(sig_te);
>
> for(i in 1:d)
> beta_sqt[i] <- sqrt(bet[i]);
> }
> model {
>
> for(i in 1:n1)
> mux[i] ~ normal(0, 1000);

You can vectorize this to

  mux ~ normal(0,1000);

But do you really have data at the scale where you expect
mux to be in the thousands?  If not, tightening the prior can
help.

> for(i in 1:n2)
> muy[i] ~ normal(0, 1000);
>
> bet ~ inv_gamma(2, 1);
> sig_lb ~ scaled_inv_chi_square(10, .1);
> sig_te ~ scaled_inv_chi_square(10, .1);


I'm not good enough to know what problems might crop up from
these priors.


> for(i in 1:d)
> Z[i] ~normal(0, 1);

all of these are vectorizable.

>
> for(i in 1:n1)
> A[i] ~ normal(0, beta_sqt);
>
> for(i in 1:n2)
> B[i] ~ normal(0, beta_sqt);

Here, you can use

   A_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

   A <- beta_sqt * A_raw;
A is a n1xd matrix and beta_sqt is a vector of d elements. Or simply put elements a given column of A have the same normal distribution. Does your suggestion still hold?

The second step can be local or implicit.

> for(j in 1:N)
> {
> for(i in 1:n1)
> {
> teta[i,j] ~ normal(mu_te[i,j] + mux[i], sigte_sr);

You can vectorize this if you transpose mu_te, as

   teta[i] ~ normal(mu_te[i] + mux, sigte_sr);

But again, you can apply the non-centered representation (aka,
the "Matt trick").  This is described in the manual.

> X[i,j] ~ poisson_log(teta[i,j]);

Yes, you can do:

   X[i] ~ poisson_log(teta[i]);

> }
> for(k in 1:n2)
> {
> lambd[k,j] ~ normal(mu_lb[k,j] + muy[k], siglb_sr);
> Y[k,j] ~ poisson_log(lambd[k,j]);
> }
> }
> }

The issue may be more related to the sampling than to the speed.
Are you getting good numbers of effective samples per iteration?

- Bob

I thought I checked that they were vectors. If they're
matrices, you still need to have one outer loop for the A_raw
sampling because we've only vectorized for vectors. But the
beta_sqt * A_raw can be done on the matrix.

- Bob
